findings.title: Server response time (TTFB) is very high at 1.45 seconds
findings.explanation: The site took about 1450 milliseconds just to start sending data, before any content even begins loading. A healthy response is usually under 200-600 milliseconds. Visitors and search engines both perceive this as a slow site, which can hurt conversions and search rankings. There's also no CDN in front of the site, so every visitor hits the origin server directly.
findings.recommendation: Investigate backend performance (database queries, app code, hosting resources) and consider adding a CDN or caching layer to reduce response time.

findings.title: Responses are marked as never cacheable
findings.explanation: The site sends a 'cache-control: no-store' header, which tells browsers and any intermediate caches to never store a copy of the page. Combined with the slow response time, this means every single visit forces a full, slow trip to the server with no chance of a faster cached load.
findings.recommendation: Review whether no-store is intentional; for pages that don't contain sensitive or personalized data, allow caching (e.g. cache-control: public, max-age=...) to improve load speed.

findings.title: TLS certificate expires in 60 days
findings.explanation: The site's SSL/TLS certificate (issued by Let's Encrypt) is valid and currently has about 60 days left before it expires. This isn't urgent yet, but Let's Encrypt certificates are short-lived and need regular renewal.
findings.recommendation: Confirm automatic renewal is configured for the certificate so it doesn't lapse.

findings.title: Email anti-spoofing records (SPF and DMARC) are properly configured
findings.explanation: The domain has a strict SPF record (v=spf1 -all) and a DMARC policy set to quarantine, which helps prevent attackers from sending fake emails that appear to come from this domain.
findings.recommendation: No action needed; continue monitoring DMARC reports if collected.
